issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who enters possession under a derivative title from a grantee must establish the elements of adverse possession against the State, including a hostile claim disclaimed from the derivative title and brought to the State’s knowledge.
material_facts: The purchasers acquired the land through sale deeds from the original grantees, whose grants restricted alienation.
Their pleadings stated that they remained in possession and enjoyment after purchase but did not plead that they had disclaimed their derivative title or asserted a hostile title against the State.
There was no evidence that they had continuously possessed the land while asserting a hostile claim against the State to its knowledge.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers did not establish adverse possession against the State, and their claim could not defeat the proceedings to recover the granted land.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be nec vi, clam, nec precario, with possession adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent to show hostility to the true owner. A purchaser who entered under a derivative title must plead and prove when and how that title was disclaimed, and that a hostile claim was asserted to the State’s knowledge without action by the State within the prescribed period. This follows R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka, applying the principles in Lakshmi Reddy, State for India v. Debendra Lal Khan, Kshitish Chandra, and Danappa Revappa Kolli v. Gurupadappa Kallappa Patana Shetti.

rule.if: appeal_from_granted_land_recovery_proceeding and purchaser_entered_under_grantee_title and no_hostile_disclaimer_pleaded and no_hostile_claim_to_state_proved

predicates.appeal_from_granted_land_recovery_procee: The case is an appeal arising from proceedings to recover land granted subject to restrictions on transfer.
predicates.purchaser_entered_under_grantee_title: The claimant entered possession through a transfer from the original grantee.
predicates.no_hostile_disclaimer_pleaded: The claimant did not plead that they disclaimed the title under which they entered and asserted a hostile title.
predicates.no_hostile_claim_to_state_proved: The claimant did not prove that a hostile claim was asserted to the State’s knowledge.

issues.definition: When a purchaser in an appeal arising from recovery of granted land entered under the grantee’s title but neither pleaded a hostile disclaimer nor proved a hostile claim to the State, the adverse-possession claim fails.

issues.legal_issue: A person other than the original grantee who possesses granted land bears the burden of rebutting the presumption that the land was acquired through a transfer prohibited by law.
material_facts: The land was granted to persons belonging to a protected class.
The purchasers, who were not the original grantees or their legal heirs, possessed the land under sale deeds.
The purchasers did not establish that their acquisition was through a transfer that was not null and void.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers bore the burden of proving that their acquisition was not through a null and void transfer, and they failed to discharge it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(3) of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act presumes, until the contrary is proved, that a person other than the original grantee or the grantee’s legal heir acquired granted land through a transfer null and void under Section 4(1). The Court held that the purchasers had not rebutted that presumption.

predicates.proceeding_under_protective_granted_land: The case concerns proceedings under a law protecting granted land against prohibited transfers.
predicates.non_grantee_in_possession_of_granted_lan: A person other than the original grantee or the grantee’s legal heir possesses the granted land.

issues.definition: In a protective granted-land proceeding, when a non-grantee possesses the land, that possessor bears the burden of proving a valid acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer contrary to restrictive terms of a grant does not confer valid title on the purchaser.
material_facts: The land was granted subject to a prohibition on alienation, which applied permanently.
The original grantees sold the land in violation of the grant restrictions.
The purchasers relied on those sales as the source of their title.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers acquired no valid title under the prohibited sales, and their possession under those sales did not establish title against the State.
issues.legal_principle: The Act’s Section 4(1) treats transfers made in contravention of the terms of a grant as null and void and provides that no right, title, or interest is conveyed by them. The Court relied on R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka and Papaiah v. State of Karnataka, and on the protective purpose reflected in Articles 39(b) and 46 of the Constitution; it also referred to Section 23 of the Contract Act. It distinguished K.T. Hutchegowda v. Deputy Commissioner, in which the relevant question had not been raised or considered.

predicates.granted_land_recovery_proceeding: The case concerns recovery of land that was granted subject to restrictions.
predicates.grant_prohibited_alienation: The terms of the grant prohibited alienation of the land.
predicates.sale_violated_grant_restriction: The grantee sold the land contrary to the restriction in the grant.

issues.definition: When a grant prohibited alienation and the grantee sold the land in violation of that restriction in a proceeding to recover the granted land, the transfer conveys no valid title.
